claims.text: The WTaTiVZr alloy is equimolar, corresponding to approximately 20 at.% of each constituent element.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater high-temperature plastic strain than commercially pure tungsten.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater high-temperature fracture toughness than commercially pure tungsten.
The WTaTiVZr alloy contains intrinsic atomic-scale chemical heterogeneity and lattice distortions.
Commercially pure tungsten has a relatively homogeneous crystalline structure compared with WTaTiVZr.
Atomic-scale heterogeneity in WTaTiVZr generates heterogeneous local stress fields.
The heterogeneous local stress fields suppress localized dislocation pile-up in WTaTiVZr.
The heterogeneous local stress fields promote activation of multiple slip systems in WTaTiVZr.
Suppressed dislocation pile-up and activation of multiple slip systems produce more uniform plastic deformation.
More uniform plastic deformation delays crack initiation in WTaTiVZr relative to pure tungsten.
Under identical high-temperature loading, WTaTiVZr will show more spatially distributed dislocation activity than pure tungsten.
Under identical high-temperature loading, WTaTiVZr will show more evidence of multiple-slip-system activation than pure tungsten.
The proposed mechanism is operative only at high temperatures where dynamic dislocation processes and slip-system activation are active.
Temperatures above approximately 800 degrees Celsius are treated as the applicable high-temperature regime.
The mechanism may not remain relevant at lower temperatures or when significant oxidation or another competing degradation process dominates.
Comparing similarly processed WTaTiVZr and pure-tungsten specimens under identical temperature, strain-rate, and atmospheric conditions is intended to isolate the effect of alloy heterogeneity.
Failure to observe statistically significant improvements in both plastic strain and toughness, or failure to observe the proposed dislocation signatures, would falsify the hypothesis.
